REPORT ON MEETING WITH B.C. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister indicated the day before yesterday that following the talks with the government of British Columbia on the matter of the Columbia river treaty I would be making a statement.
Pursuant to this undertaking I should like to say that late yesterday representatives of the government completed two days of talks about the development of the Columbia river with representatives of the provincial government of British Columbia. The house will not, I am sure, expect an exhaustive report at this stage while matters are still under negotiation. I can, however, say that the main objective of the talks was to prepare the way for the basic agreement between the federal and provincial governments which will be necessary if further progress is to be made in the co-operative development of the water resources of the Columbia river basin. It seems to me only prudent that such a firm understanding with the British Columbia government should be secured before final negotiations with the United States are resumed. I can say, too, that the British Columbia government is in full accord with this view.

At the conclusion of the meeting late last night the following communique was issued:
Yesterday and today, talks regarding the Columbia river treaty have been taking place between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia at the ministerial and official levels. The British Columbia delegation was led by Premier Bennett and the federal delegation was led by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Associated with them were, for British Columbia, Hon. Robert Bonner, Hon. Ray Williston and senior officers of the British Columbia hydro and power authority and the British Columbia water resources service and for Canada, Hon. Arthur Laing, Hon. John R. Nicholson, Dr. Jack Davis and Dr. John Stewart and officials of the federal departments concerned.
Following a joint meeting with Prime Minister Pearson, the two delegations have held a series of intensive discussions on various aspects of the treaty and on the arrangements which would be required between the Canadian government and the British Columbia government.
The provincial and federal representatives have had a thorough discussion on the modifications and clarifications in the treaty which Prime Minister Pearson had suggested to President Kennedy in their meeting at Hyannis Port last month. The representatives of British Columbia and of the federal government considered that these improvements should be sought through some device such as a protocol to the existing treaty which would not involve the renegotiation of the treaty itself. In particular, the two delegations agreed that the price and other terms of sale for Canada's downstream power benefits generated in the United States should be further negotiated before any exchange of instruments of ratification which would bring the treaty into force. Such an exchange of instruments of ratification would, of course, only take place after action has been completed by the Canadian government and the Canadian parliament.
In addition to discussions on the treaty itself, during several working sessions the federal and provincial representatives drafted the provisions of an agreement designed to set out clearly the responsibilities of the federal and provincial governments and to ensure that all of the arrangements under the treaty bring the maximum advantage to the people of British Columbia and the rest of

Columbia River Treaty
Canada. The agreement is based on the intention that the necessary modifications will be negotiated in the proposed treaty arrangements and that the way will then be open for ratification of the treaty. The agreement drafted over the past two days is being submitted to the two governments for their consideration.
Final decisions on the various matters, including the draft agreement, discussed during the present series of meetings can only be taken by the federal and provincial governments after they have had an opportunity to consider the reports from their representatives. The meetings have taken place in a co-operative and constructive atmosphere. Both delegations were anxious to make as much progress as possible.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING WITH B.C. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the concluding words of the communique that was issued will be shared by all hon. members. We, of course, have had some experience since January, 1960 in that connection. A number of meetings were held between the government of Canada and the government of British Columbia. They were amicable and constructive but they ended without agreement.
It is well to look back over the years and realize that in January, 1960 when the treaty was signed it represented the consensus not only of the government of Canada but of the government of British Columbia. The government of British Columbia was represented. It agreed to the terms, the treaty was signed, and it was only then that disagreements arose as the result of a desire on the part of the government of British Columbia to have terms different from those already agreed on.
All of us would welcome proceeding with the development of the Columbia. At the same time the Peace river project is now under way. When these two projects are under way and power is developed, naturally the house will want to know what provision is going to be made for the marketing of what will be bound to be a tremendous surplus of power. Will there be action taken on the part of the federal government to bring about that which we advocated, namely a national grid to assure that future generations of Canadians will have available to them the vast power potentialities of our country?
Then, in so far as downstream benefits are concerned, the communique is veiled in uncertainty. Apparently the sale of these benefits is to depend on the price secured in the United States. We have always contended that, in so far as downstream benefits are concerned, if they mean as we believe they do, cheaper power, the major portion of the downstream benefits should be made available to Canadians. This phase of the situation was not dealt with except in generalities.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).I
I welcome the fine spirit that has prevailed as between the representatives of the federal government and the provincial government, but I point out this on the basis of experience in the past. Unless the government of Canada will do that which Premier Bennett wants done, agreement cannot be secured. In other words, if agreement is secured he will be the one who will determine the terms of the agreement.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING WITH B.C. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we certainly do welcome the announcement today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs concerning the arrangements that have been discussed with the government of British Columbia. I should like to say it is my opinion that we have had some of the top men in Canada participating in these discussions on this subject. I am confident from the fact that we are now getting action in connection with this treaty, that the words of the former prime minister, now the Leader of the Opposition, sound very hollow indeed. The political implications of what has taken place in British Columbia in recent months certainly must show us in this house what some of the real stumbling blocks were in connection with getting anything done about the Columbia river.
We have now seen some action in connection with this matter. I am certain that with the type of individuals who are actually engaged in the negotiations we will be pleased, not only as people of British Columbia but as people of Canada, when the final arrangements are made. I have every confidence that this will be so.
In so far as the premier of British Columbia wanting his own way is concerned, why shouldn't he? Since he is the premier of British Columbia, he is there to represent these people, and why should he not get the best deal possible for the province of British Columbia? I am all for that. I think it is axiomatic that if he does so we will have the best possible program for the Dominion of Canada as well.
In so far as the Peace river project is concerned, I am pleased to see that the Peace river development has speeded up the need, in the general over-all picture of power, for the development of the Columbia. It is obvious that the development of the Peace river area is something that is badly needed in western Canada, and certainly a national grid to tap some of that power and bring it to the prairies and other places is something that should be considered by the government, and no doubt will be.

I appreciate very much the report that has been made, and we will be looking forward to further reports. I am sure that the $9 million which British Columbia has already spent on the Columbia river shows the province has not been lax in promoting the program and the project.

subtopic: REPORT ON MEETING WITH B.C. REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think all hon. members will agree that it is the part of wisdom to conclude an agreement with the province of British Columbia before attempting to carry on any negotiations with the government of the United States. The present impasse we are in is due to the fact that this process was not carried through.
However, Mr. Speaker, there are three points about which members of my party are concerned. I wish to say first of all to the minister that we would like to have some undertaking that those who are affected by this Columbia river treaty plan, and any modifications or changes in that plan, will be given the opportunity to be heard. To the best of my knowledge they have written assurance that, in any modification or renegotiation of the treaty, they will be given ample opportunity to express their views and to be heard. I certainly hope this commitment, which I understand was made by the Prime Minister himself, will be fulfilled to the letter. Therefore I express the hope no final decision will be reached, and no final commitments made, until the committee on external affairs has an opportunity to review the entire matter.
The second point that gives us concern is the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that negotiations are going on regarding the price of downstream power benefits. This would indicate that the principle of selling the downstream power benefits has been accepted. We certainly would have serious misgivings about the acceptance of such a principle, particularly until the whole situation has been reviewed; because there is ample evidence of the fact that it would be much more economical for Canada, as a whole, and for the lower mainland of British Columbia in particular to have this power delivered to Canadian consumers rather than having it sold to United States power companies.
The third point is that we think the treaty itself needs to be re-examined to see whether it is the best treaty negotiable to make the maximum use of the resources under discussion. Many persons have been questioning why the original McNaughton plan was dropped. I understand it was dropped because the province of British Columbia preferred
Columbia River Treaty another plan, but the committee on external affairs and this house have the right to ask that General McNaughton be called as a witness, and that other experts be called to review the McNaughton plan.
The whole question of power has obscured the much more important question of the best use of our water resources, because the entire flow of one of our largest rivers, is being sold in perpetuity. The prairies are particularly interested in this matter of water flow, and I am told that even a 10 per cent diversion of the Columbia river could double the flow of water in the Saskatchewan river. This is certainly important in a country where irrigation and water conservation are matters of growing urgency. Therefore we would expect that while these negotiations continue no commitment will be made until the external affairs committee has had a full and extensive opportunity to review any modifications and changes in the treaty before ratification of the treaty itself.

PROMOTIONS AND WORKING CONDITIONS, PENITENTIARY STAFFS
speechtext:
1.	Are promotions on penitentiary staffs made as a result of (a) seniority (b) competitive examinations or (c) both seniority and competitive examination?
2.	In 1962 and 1963, have complaints been received relative to working conditions of penitentiary staffs and, if so, what is the nature of these complaints, and what action has been undertaken to consider and correct them?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROMOTIONS AND WORKING CONDITIONS, PENITENTIARY STAFFS
speechtext:
1. Promotions of penitentiary staffs are made in accordance with P.S.R. 1.19, by competition. Written examinations are requested whenever it is considered necessary to test the applicant's technical qualifications and ability. Seniority is taken into consideration only when all other factors are considered equal.
2.	In 1962 and 1963, no individual staff complaints were received relative to working conditions of penitentiary staffs. However, the Civil Service Association of Canada made representations about:
(a)	alleged deficiencies in security and discipline at Kingston penitentiary. These were investigated and the commissioner, in his six page letter of February 14, 1962, to the national president, C.S.A.C., explained a course of action to rectify any verified deficiencies in security and discipline.
(b)	salary differentials between correctional officers (camps) and guards in main institutions. The whole penitentiary service pay structure is now under review by treasury board.
(c)	security problems at Dorchester penitentiary. These were fully investigated in January 1962, and corrective action taken by authorizing additional custodial staff.
(d)	consultation between the association and the commissioner of penitentiaries. Procedures were adopted to the satisfaction of the association.

(e)	salary schedules generally in the penitentiary service. These are now under study by treasury board.
(f)	commuting allowances for certain institutions. This is under review by treasury board.
(g)	cash payment for overtime. Where it has not been feasible to pay overtime through compensatory time off, cash payments have been made.
Ch) uniform issue schedules. This problem has been rectified as quickly as possible through production shop overtime, particularly by Leclerc institution.
(i)	perquisites allowed penitentiary officers. Treasury board, in their current review of salary schedules, has been asked to consider the whole question of perquisites.
(j)	health of penitentiary officers (contracting tuberculosis). The long standing policy of annual T.B. X-ray surveys for staff and inmates was explained to the national president, Civil Service Association of Canada.
(k)	compensation for overtime worked and also compensation for work done on a statutory holiday. Policy in this regard has been under study for some months and it is hoped a directive will be issued soon clarifying this situation.
(l)	pensions paid to widows and orphans of officers killed on duty. Changes in current legislation, particularly the Superannuation Act, would have to be made. Preliminary discussions have taken place with treasury board in this connection.
There is continuous liaison with the Civil Service Association of Canada for corrective action of legitimate staff complaints.

1.	Has the government of Canada found out whether its predecessor entered into any commitment or undertaking with NATO or any government or person involving the use by Canadian forces of nuclear warheads in Europe or in Canada?
2.	If so (a) to whom was the commitment or undertaking given (b) what were the terms of such commitment or undertaking (c) was the undertaking explicitly or by implication revocable by the government and under what conditions (d) was the commitment or undertaking in writing and what was the nature of the document
Questions
(e) by whom was it given or made, and with what authority (f) what was the date of such commitment, if any, or the ratification thereof by the former government of Canada?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
1. Yes.
2. (a), (b), (c), (d), (e), (f):
In respect of Canadian forces in Europe the undertakings arise out of NATO processes. NATO does not enter into formal agreements or treaties with member nations regarding their military contributions. The military authorities of the alliance set certain requirements and individual countries determine what contributions they will make toward meeting those requirements. The whole process is accomplished by direct discussions with the NATO commanders concerned and is confirmed in an annual review process which is secret.
The acquisition of the Honest Johns and the CF-104's and the roles planned for them were the subject of this process in 1958 and 1959 respectively.
In respect of Canadian forces in Canada the undertakings arise out of allocations made by Canada in fulfillment of the NORAD agreement.
On September 27, 1961, Canada concluded an agreement with the United States providing for improvements in the continental air defence system in Canada. This included the establishment of Bomarc squadrons in Canada. There was no specific reference to the armament to be provided for the Bomarcs but no conventional warhead was ever developed for the Bomarc "B", the type planned for siting in Canada and ultimately installed. It was understood by the government of the day that the Bomarc anti-aircraft missile, to be effective, would require nuclear warheads (cf. Prime Minister, Hansard, January 18, 1960, page 73).
On June 12, 1961, an agreement was concluded with the United States whereby Canada was furnished with 66 F-101B (Voodoo) interceptor aircraft. The agreement specified that the armament was to be mutually agreed and the aircraft as delivered was designed to carry a mixed armament of nuclear and conventional rockets. Only the conventional armament has been acquired although it was known to the government of the day that without their nuclear rockets the aircraft were not fully armed.

speechtext: The national building code of Canada 1960 includes proper provisions for earthquake design of structures throughout Canada in accordance with internationally recognized standards. subsubtopic: EFFECT ON CANADA OF U.S. DECISION
speechtext:
1.	What will be the effect on the Canadian uranium industry of the United States decision to rely on domestic sources of uranium?
2.	Will any areas of Canada be more particularly affected than others and, if so, what will be such regional effects?
3.	Will such U.S. decision result in a cut-back in Canadian production to about 1,000 tons a year from the peak of 15,000 tons in 1959?
4.	What preparations are being made to deal with the dislocations likely to take place in the uranium industry in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subsubtopic: EFFECT ON CANADA OF U.S. DECISION
speechtext:
1. The United States has not made a definite decision to rely on domestic sources of uranium. The general demand for uranium in the western world has fallen and it has been necessary to close mines not only in Canada but also in the United States, South Africa, Australia, Portugal and elsewhere.
At the moment domestic production in the United States is more than sufficient for their national requirements. This condition will last until the late sixties when it is expected that there will be an increase in the western world's requirement for uranium, and the U.S. needs may then exceed local production.
2. No one area in Canada will be affected relatively more than another. The firm contracts now held for delivery of uranium to

the U.S. atomic energy commission and the U.K. atomic energy authority terminate on different dates, which will cause closure of mines earlier in some areas than in others. The varying closing dates are due to the time of the signing of the original contracts and to the efforts that some companies have made over the last three years to stretch out their operations.
3.	Canadian production of uranium will drop to less than 2,000 tons by 1967 unless new contracts are written, but this is due to the termination of the firm contracts written a number of years ago and not to a recent decision.
4.	The Canadian government is urgently examining the effect of the closures of the uranium mines on the communities directly concerned.

1.	Where do negotiations stand on an international sugar agreement?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
1. The 1958 international sugar agreement is to expire December 31st, 1963.
The operative provisions of the present agreement have not been in force since January 1, 1962, owing to the inability of the review international sugar conference to arrive at agreement in Geneva during September and October, 1961. Primarily disagreement stemmed from the insistance of Cuba to be allowed to export a sugar quota in excess of what appeared to the conference to be a realistic figure.
At a meeting of the international sugar council in London during the first week of April, the member governments concluded that it was not possible under present circumstances to negotiate a new agreement with meaningful marketing controls or export quotas. It was, therefore, agreed that, notwithstanding the suspension of the operative provisions of the agreement, it would be
desirable to maintain the administrative provisions and to continue the useful work being performed by the international sugar council.
During the first week of July, 1963, the secretary general of the United Nations will convene a short conference in London, England, to establish a protocol prolonging the present international sugar agreement without provisions for export quotas or controls.
The protocol is to prolong the agreement until December 31, 1964, or December 31, 1965, whichever of the dates the conference will decide. This protocol will enter into force on January 1, 1964, provided a sufficient number of member governments sign. Instruments of ratification, acceptance or accession will take effect on the date of their deposit. If it is determined that less than the required number (to be determined by the conference), of countries have become parties to this protocol by January 1, 1964, the governments which have signed, ratified, accepted or acceded to this protocol may agree to put it into force among themselves.
2. In view of the forthcoming meeting in July of the international sugar conference, it is not possible at this time to indicate those nations which are opposed to the international

[Editor's Note: The document above referred to is as follows:]
Early in May, the Northwest Territories communities of Hay River and Fort Simpson suffered serious flooding. It was necessary to evacuate both communities; about 1,500 people left Hay River and about 650 left Fort Simpson.
The people evacuated from these two communities represent about 10 per cent of the population of the Northwest Territories. Most of them went to Yellowknife and Fort Smith which have a combined population of about 6,000. While the numbers are small, the proportions are startling; moving 2,000 into these communities is roughly equivalent to moving 100,000 on very short notice into Ottawa and Hull.
The evacuation was carried out without a single casualty or serious injury-a tremendous tribute to the people of both these communities and to those others-helicopter and air line personnel, local community leaders, the R.C.M.P. and other government agencies,

Inquiries of the Ministry the defence forces, and indeed virtually everyone who was directly or indirectly concerned with the operation. One must mention also the people of Yellowknife and Fort Smith who opened their hearts and their homes to the evacuees.
As soon as the scale of the disaster was apparent, arrangements were put in hand to re-establish the two damaged communities.
Immediately following the floods, arrangements were made for a team of assessors to appraise the damage. In accordance with normal practice, the damage was assessed on the depreciated value of the assets at the time of the flood. In other words, appraised damage is much lower than replacement cost.
The preliminary report to the appraisers shows total damage at Hay River of $614,573. This does not include damage to ships and barges and some relatively small items on which the appraisal is not yet complete.
While the situation at Fort Simpson was very serious, the actual damage was not as great as had at first been feared. The appraisers' report has not yet been received, but it seems likely that the figure will be of the order of $50,000. None of these figures, incidentally, include damage to federal property; they do include damage to business property and equipment as well as to private property and personal effects.
Under our Canadian constitutional practice, the primary responsibility for dealing with disasters of this kind rests with the provincial government concerned-or, in this case, with the government of the Northwest Territories. The federal government at once indicated its willingness to stand behind the territorial government, which has very limited resources of its own, in any reasonable arrangements which it might make for the compensation of flood victims.
The council of the Northwest Territories accordingly met in special session in Hay River on May 15 and May 17. The council appropriated $100,000-all that it could reasonably afford-toward the expenses of evacuation and rehabilitation.
The council also established a compensation policy which involves in summary contributions towards the cost of replacing or rebuilding damaged property on the following scale:
Personal real property-100 per cent of appraised loss.
Clothes, furniture, and other personal effects-80 per cent of appraised loss.
Commercial stock in trade-70 per cent of appraised loss.
Other business losses-80 per cent of appraised loss.


In the light of limited funds available, the council decided that compensation for business losses should be limited to individuals and firms carrying on their business wholly or largely in the disaster area.
Since this subject may be of interest to some members of the house, Mr. Speaker, I would ask leave to table copies of the statement of policy approved by the commissioner in council at its meeting on May 17.
As indicated earlier, the federal government has agreed to provide such financial support as may be necessary to enable the territorial government to carry out this compensation policy.
On May 27, a compensation office staffed by treasury officers from Edmonton was established in Hay River. This office is prepared to issue payments to flood victims in accordance with the policy established by the council and started writing cheques on May 30. (On May 30 and 31, payments totalled approximately $15,000). Preliminary reports from Hay River indicate that the procedure is operating reasonably smoothly and quickly.
The Northwest Territories council also arranged for a new subdivision on the mainland to be developed for occupancy this year.
In my view, Mr. Speaker, the arrangements and policies established by the Northwest Territories government and supported by the government of Canada represent reasonable and generous financial support for the people of Hay River and Fort Simpson. However, we must recognize that there will be losses which government assistance cannot cover. To help in this regard, a Northwest Territories flood relief fund has been established under private auspices. It is my hope that this fund will help to relieve some of the hardship which inevitably results from a disaster of this kind.

The house resumed, from Tuesday, June 4, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson:
That a special committee be appointed to consider matters relating to defence and to report from time to time its observations and opinions thereon; that the committee have power to send for persons, papers and records and to examine witnesses; that it be empowered to adjourn from place to place; that standing order 67 be suspended in relation to the committee; and that the committee consist of 24 members to be designated by the house at a later date.

Before a defence committee is established, we would be very glad if the Associate Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cardin), or the Prime Minister were to inform the house of the present government's intention concerning the defence policy.
In my opinion, this suggestion would serve the interest of the country. A committee to IMr. Speaker.]

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this motion and offer a few opinions and make a few suggestions. First of all I must say that I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) say that the committee would have an opportunity to discuss policy. However, my former experience on defence committees leads me to be less optimistic than some hon. members of this house as to what will result from this promise that the committee members can discuss policy. At the same time, I am not quite as cynical as some others have been in the debate with respect to this offer on the part of the Prime Minister. My attitude at this time in that respect is simply to wait and see. It is a question of, once bitten, twice shy.

Whenever questions relating to defence expenditures are under consideration in this house I am reminded of a statement made by the former hon. member, Major General Pearkes, V.C., who I am sure all hon. members will admit spoke as a result of long army experience and a long interest in matters military. I remember him on one occasion rising in the house and saying:
I have never in all my experience known an admiral or a general or an air marshal who did not ask for far more than he required.
I have repeated that statement, Mr. Speaker; it is more or less a text with which I have prefaced my speeches on defence estimates throughout the years. I would urge the committee to keep those famous words constantly in mind when listening to the pleas of those who follow in the tradition of those whom Major General Pearkes mentioned.
The opposition of this party to nuclear weapons is based on moral, military and economic grounds. The reasons for this opposition have been stated in excellent manner by our leader, and in a most eloquent speech last evening by the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron). Correspondence, resolutions and editorials indicate a widespread concern with the moral aspects of this question. Let me say that although we have had a vote in this house, the present government is not free of discussion in the country with respect to its decision to accept nuclear weapons for our defence forces.
In that connection, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote from an editorial in the Victoria Colonist which I think puts the question very well indeed. The article is headed "Nuclear burden" and says:
When the Canadian air division is fully operational it will have the nuclear capability of destroying the equivalent of 600 Hiroshimas, killing 48 million people and injuring another 22 million. In other words the R.C.A.F. European air division will be hundreds of times more powerful than the combined strengths of all the allied armed forces used in the second world war.
Under optimum conditions Canada's air division could, for instance, completely obliterate the British Isles, or Germany, or even a large part of the U.S.S.R. To be in possession of, and responsible for such enormous destructive power imposes an almost impossible responsibility upon any nation. And such a burden is now Canada's.

SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF MORTGAGE PROVISIONS TO INCLUDE COMPLETED DWELLINGS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of amending the provisions of the National Housing Act so that the mortgage provisions of the said act be extended to the purchase and sale of homes and dwellings that have already been completed and occupied.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to the motion I should first like to make clear to hon. members of the house what I am hoping to achieve by presenting this motion to the house. It is essentially an attempt to end the discrimination that has been practised by successive governments in Canada, under the provisions of the National Housing Act, between the suburbs and the cities which are hemmed in. by these suburbs. What I am attempting to do in the resolution is to make the same financial mortgage arrangements available to people in our cities who wish to purchase older homes in the cities and live there. I am trying to see that they have the same financial arrangements with respect to the purchasing of their homes as those who live in the suburbs. I myself live in suburbia outside the city of Toronto and I enjoy it, but I realize that there are thousands and thousands of Canadians from coast to coast who would prefer to purchase a home and live their lives in the cities. What I should like to see is the provisions of the National Housing Act amended so that its mortgage arrangements can be extended to those who wish to live in our cities.
There are many factors in the National Housing Act which we should like to examine, and no doubt there will be a more appropriate time provided later for us to make this examination. I have deliberately restricted this motion to the very narrow ground I have outlined because it is one of the provisions of the National Housing Act that has always seemed to me completely

indefensible and actually silly. I do hope hon. members of the Progressive Conservative party who may speak in this hour devoted to this resolution will give us some indication why such a proposal was never accepted during their term of office.
Mr. Speaker, if one looks at the present situation the National Housing Act financing arrangements are restricted to homes which have not as yet been constructed. If you wish to purchase a home under the National Housing Act you have to have a vacant piece of land, take your plans to the local C.M.H.C. office, and if they approve them you can get a mortgage covering 90 per cent of the purchase price of the house. Since pretty well all the vacant land is outside our large cities, and since most of the vacant land inside the cities does not meet National Housing Act requirements, this in effect means that almost all the financing of individual dwellings in Canada under the provisions of the National Housing Act is restricted to new homes being built in the suburbs surrounding most of our major cities. This is not a criticism of the C.M.H.C. officials themselves but it has been the policy of successive governments that this should be the case. What this means is that if a young couple, or any other couple for that matter, wish to remain within our cities and to live there, they cannot obtain the advantages of the financing arrangements of the National Housing Act. If they want to buy a house with a low down payment and a mortgage they can adequately carry, they are forced to leave the cities and to move out into the sprawling miles and miles of suburbia. To me this seems to be a totally unfair form of discrimination which cannot in any way be defended or justified. I know that many hon. members in this house who have dealt with conveyancing problems in their private practices have run up against the many difficulties which this situation creates.
As to why a change is needed, one of the difficulties, as I have said, is that because the National Housing Act is administered in this fashion all of the new homes are being built in our suburbs. This has resulted over the years in a very strong push from the cities out into the suburbs by most of our young couples. This has created for our municipalities tremendous problems in meeting the demands which new houses create-demands for roads, schools, curbs, water mains and all the other facilities which must be made available for new housing. The result to the municipalities has been an ever increasing and indeed a crushing tax load to meet these urgent requirements.
This is particularly evident in the administration and the supplying of school facilities.

I understand that every 40 new homes creates a demand for a new schoolroom at a cost to the municipality of some $40,000. The mushrooming growth of our municipalities, and the school requirements this has created, has in itself imposed a tremendous debt burden and great financial problems on all local municipalities. I do not know why this should be the case except that most of the people moving to the suburbs seem to be young, and begin to raise very large families, which creates this schooling problem.
Another difficulty which this method of N.H.A. financing creates is the problem of young people in our cities who want to buy a house. For example, Mr. Speaker, if you wanted to buy a house costing $12,000 and live in one of our cities, you could only get a first mortgage of about $6,000. Therefore, unless a young couple has $6,000 in cash they either cannot afford to buy the house or else they have to buy whatever equity in it they can and give back a large second mortgage. Second mortgages run from five to ten years and create additional carrying costs for the young couple. When these mortgages mature at the end of five or ten years they have to be renewed if the young couple cannot pay them off. They are renewed with a bonus, which usually just about equals the amount of principal which has been paid off. There are many cases in my constituency, and I am sure in many others, where young couples are buying houses with second mortgages on them, and they will never own them because every time the mortgage is renewed the bonus attached equals the amount of money they have paid off the mortgage, so they will go on in perpetuity buying these houses and will never really own them.
Another matter which would be of advantage in this proposal is that under the National Housing Act the mortgages run for 25 to 30 years. This would be a tremendous advantage to young people buying homes. It would give a great degree of stability to their home buying. It would enable them to budget their income over a longer period of time and would enable them to plan their families and their entire married life together. Another thing it would do is to make these homes easier to resell. If a young couple today buys a house in the city they will find that after living in the house for four or five years the property is virtually unable to be resold because purchasers simply will not buy these older homes with second mortgages running out in one or two years after they purchase. So that the provision of N.H.A. financing for older homes in our cities would go a long way not only to help out the second mortgage victimization which is now taking place in Canada but would make it easier for young
National Housing Act
couples to resell their homes in the event that they wanted to move somewhere else.
There have been some moves in Canada recently to provide the higher mortgage financing which N.H.A. does not provide. There are some companies in Toronto who will give a mortgage of 80 per cent of the value of a new home. The only difficulty is that the interest charged is 8 per cent, which is much too high a rate for a young couple to be able adequately to carry. Indeed, I hope that at some stage we will be able to discuss the whole question of interest rates under the National Housing Act. For example, if you have a mortgage on your home at 6J per cent under N.H.A., this is what it costs you. If the amount of the mortgage is $14,400, at 6f per cent over 25 years you will actually pay back $29,366. If that same $14,400 mortgage is stretched over 30 years you will actually pay back $33,084. This represents a mortgage interest rate of 6f per cent, and I leave to the imagination of hon. members the fantastic return which would be made if they were to finance a home in Toronto at the present time and pay 8 per cent over 25 or 30 years. One would be paying something like $14,000 over 25 years. Action along the lines I have suggested should make it easier for people to live in the cities and to buy their homes there. Favourable comment on this proposal has come from sources almost too numerous to mention, including builders associations, many of the construction industries and real estate companies, such reputable journals as the Globe and Mail and the Toronto Daily Star and community planners. All have recommended that steps of this kind should be taken. Even the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Garland) while he was in opposition spoke eloquently in favour of this provision and I am sure he has not changed his views since and that I can count on his support.
In actual fact, the question is not whether this should be done but why it has not been done in the past. The present system of home financing is discriminatory and under present conditions it can no longer be justified. It was all right when the National Housing Act first came into being because at that time what we primarily wanted was new housing. But now conditions have changed and the time has come to reconsider the act. People should have freedom of choice regarding where they are to live-whether they are to live in the city or in the suburbs. At present the choice is weighted heavily in favour of suburban living. An extension of the provisions of N.H.A. into the cities would relieve pressure in the suburbs. It would relieve householders of second mortgage victimization and, in particular, it would help young people

National Housing Act
who are seeking homes. There are thousands of reasons which could be advanced in favour of this proposition but I do not wish to spend too much time discussing them because I should like to hear the views of other hon. members on this proposal.
I realize that in the hour we have available we cannot, obviously, consider all the ramifications of such a proposal as I have made. However, I think the resolution in principle merits support by hon. members. I should like to suggest that, following approval of the principle, by unanimous consent it be referred to the committee on banking and commerce in order that hon. members may consider it, call in witnesses and hear the views of experts. With the co-operation of all hon. members we could then draw up a bill which would meet all difficulties, and bring it back for consideration at a later time.
I want to review an appeal which was made the other day in this private members' hour that serious consideration be given to paying greater attention to the matters which private members raise during this period. I hope we can do away with the farcical treatment which private members receive in this house. When we go to our constituencies and tell our constituents that every day we spend an hour debating private members' business, that everybody loves the bill under discussion to death, that everybody spends so much time saying how much they are in favour of it but that no action is ever taken and the measure is dropped to the end of a long list and never to be heard of again-when we explain all this to our constituents it is no wonder they ask themselves why we conduct our business in such a witless manner.

In the British house of commons private members' bills do proceed after consideration to the stages of third reading and royal assent. Hon. members in all quarters of the house have matters of great importance to put forward for consideration. Many of the motions and bills put forward contain good ideas, and it seems to me that a motion such as this should receive assent and go to a committee where the views of all hon. members could be taken into consideration and where a considered piece of legislation could be assembled. I hope this can be done and

that my proposal will be sent to a committee where it will receive full consideration.

speechtext:
In speaking to this resolution I should like to assure the hon. gentleman who has proposed it that it is my intention to give it serious treatment. I believe that the matter dealt with in this resolution is a serious one, and one of great import.
My own particular riding, as the hon. member probably knows, is a riding which could benefit greatly from the sort of change he proposes. We are a downtown urban riding where many of the houses are old. We do not have a suburbia. I know, as the hon. member has stated, that many of the people who live in my riding are paying first mortgages, and very high interest rates on second mortgages to try to own their homes. I also know that this presents a great problem to some of these people. There is a problem of mobility. Children get married, and parents are then stuck with a house which is too large for their needs but difficult to sell. There is no mobility, because financing is not available. I know, also, that the young people who move out of these homes are forced to go into the suburbs if they want to own their homes. This gives rise to all sorts of problems, including that of transportation to and from work, and possibly getting them involved financially in the purchase of a car and other things they would like to stay away from.
I also recognize that in making financing available in respect of older homes we would help to some degree the sale of new homes because it would allow for trade-ins on new homes. This would allow a certain mobility as between owners of old and new houses. The steps which the hon. member suggests would be very desirable, particularly bearing in mind the needs of my own riding. It is a step which during the election campaign I advocated strongly, and it is something I still advocate.
However, I must add that during the election campaign I also advocated that we must approach our legislative program with responsibility and that the first thing which should receive our attention is the problem of unemployment. We should try to solve this problem first and make it the first call on our resources and on our available dollars. When we get that problem under control we can turn to these other highly desirable social measures. It seems to me, then, that in considering this measure we must ask ourselves how it would fit in with our policy for dealing with the fundamental problem of unemployment. We must ask ourselves whether, in terms of priority, we can

link it with the measures designed to improve the employment position, or whether it ought to be held back for a period.
It appears to me that the first thing we should consider is the background of our housing legislation. The hon. member mentioned that this legislation tended to be discriminatory and he suggested there was no reasoning behind the legislation as it is now drafted. I take exception to that. It is true the legislation is discriminatory and that it does aid the people who want to buy new homes as opposed to those who wish to buy an existing house. But that is for a very good reason. I think the financing which has been available in respect of new housing has played an important part in supporting employment in the construction industry by enabling new houses to be built and I think we must all realize that this is an important source of employment in our country. Thus, we have to be careful that whatever we do to improve the situation with respect to the purchase of older homes we should not sap the vital strength necessary in order to assist new home building projects. If we were to do that it would have serious consequences on the employment picture.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Act now operates in a number of fields and I should like to give quickly from their annual report some indication of the sort of things they are doing. They are insuring mortgage loans on new housing made by banks and conventional institutions. They are also making, as we all know, direct loans for new houses. They are also working in the field of limited dividend housing where the purpose is to try to meet social need by providing rental accommodation at low rental rates. They are making loans to universities to assist in providing dormitory accommodation for resident students. They are making loans to municipalities to help them work on their municipal sewage problems. They are also doing another important thing which does get down to the area of older homes. They are providing insurance to banks on home improvement loans. This means that people who own older homes are not completely barred from help. They are at least able to make improvements to their homes with bank loans insured under N.H.A.
There are a number of other projects which Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is working on, but broadly speaking the purpose of the legislation has been a dual one. The first purpose is to try to provide social help in the housing field, to try to meet the needs of the people with regard to housing.
National Housing Act
It has as its second aim, and this is very important, the assisting of the construction industry with respect to new housing and thus helping to provide jobs in that industry.
I want to give some figures so we will have some idea of the scope of the problem about which we are talking. In 1962 there were about 130,000 residential units constructed. This represents $1,587 million. Bear in mind that this is a substantial sum of money. Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation provided financing for 48,000 units or roughly 30-odd per cent of the total. Of these 48,000 units, 32,000 were financed by conventional lending institutions insured under N.H.A. and 16,000 were direct loans under N.H.A. In addition, N.H.A. provided $21 million for university housing, $45 million in the field of sewage treatment and $3 million in the field of urban redevelopment. It guaranteed loans to the banks in the amount of $38 million for home improvements and in the field of new construction $384 million was lent on new housing through N.H.A. of which $163 million represented direct loans by N.H.A.
What does all this tell us? I think it tells us a couple of things. As I have said before, I think it tells us that the housing act is moving into areas of housing other than straight new construction. I think it tells us something about the amount of money involved. When we look at the dollars that we have pumped in, $383 million under N.H.A. into the construction of new homes, $45 million in the field of sewage treatment and $38 million in the field of home improvements, I think it tells us that the housing act has pumped a lot of money into employment creating activities, and this is something we must make sure continues.
During the recent election campaign the party to which the hon. member who proposed this notice of motion belongs was talking about massive doses of social capital being required to go to work on our unemployment problem. I consider the funds that have been pumped in under N.H.A. to be just that very thing, massive doses of social capital working in the field of unemployment. Our new government is working to try to solve the unemployment problem. We are proposing a municipal loan fund, we are proposing an Atlantic development board, we are proposing a national development corporation and a number of other measures. I think these things all have one factor in common and that is that they too are going to require large sums of money. We know, for instance, that the municipal loan fund is going to take $400 million. When we add to this the fact that we have had large deficits in the last few years and despite the skill of our new Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) will probably have a

National Housing Act
deficit this year, I think we must realize that the problem of the federal government and Canada as a country is similar to that of any municipality or individual, namely that the amount of money you can borrow, the amount of debt you can carry, is limited. You can only go so far.
When we look at the problems we have I think we must realize that if we are going to tackle this business of trying to make loans available for older houses we are probably going to be restricted in the number of dollars we can use in the housing field to something approaching the level that we had last year. This being the case, if we are unable to put more money into this area and if we then make loans available for older homes we do so at the risk of siphoning money away from the field of new construction, at the risk of cutting down in this field which is providing so much in the way of employment. Therefore I think this is the first consideration, and a consideration that to me makes this desirable move one that must take its proper place in priority. In other words, I think it is highly desirable that we do it but we must do it at a time when we can put enough new money into this field so that we do not at the same time detract from the construction of new houses.
There is another thing that I think we have to look at and that is some of the ramifications of what we do. I admit this is a relatively secondary issue as far as I am concerned. If we put money into older homes and make financing available-

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF MORTGAGE PROVISIONS TO INCLUDE COMPLETED DWELLINGS
speechtext:
If you will allow me to finish I will be quite pleased to answer them.
If we make funds available for our older homes we have got to be careful that we do not make funds available for older homes on a rental basis. I think we have got to be sure that we do not encourage people to buy up with government financing a bunch of older homes in a downtown area and keep them in a rundown condition, and in effect run a rental slum empire. If we make funds available to people for older homes I think it is very important that we try to make sure or at least consider whether we should make sure that these funds go to the owners of homes rather than to a landlord who is going to rent. I think we could get into trouble if we allowed people to buy up with low cost N.H.A. loans a lot of older homes, keep them in a rundown condition, rent them at low rental rates and in effect perpetuate slum districts. There are other problems of that type.

To my mind these are problems that are involved in the mechanics of working out the extension of this type of financing to older homes. I believe these problems require study but I think they are soluble. However, in my opinion one problem that is not immediately soluble is that involved on the one hand, in the restricted amount of money that can go into this field and, on the other hand, in not taking away from the existing level of new building construction.
I have just one more point in this regard. Probably about two thirds of the funds that went into housing last year under N.H.A. came from conventional lenders. The balance is made up of direct loans from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
I think it is a safe assumption that conventional lenders would prefer to continue to lend in the new housing field rather than in the area of older homes. This means that the need for funds in this area would have to be met in higher proportion by direct N.H.A. loans. I think it is a reasonable assumption, therefore, that to implement this program, if we are not going to take funds from our present home-building field, we are going to have to provide greater sums of money. I feel that just as soon as we can possibly implement this program it should be one with top priority. I hope that as soon as we can provide the funds in this area this government will do so, because it is something that is essential, it is something that is vital and it is something that I strongly support. I do recognize that it must be done at a time when it can be done properly, when funds can reasonably be made available for this purpose. I hope that time will not be very long in coming.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman was kind enough to indicate that he would reply to a question at the end of his remarks. In his speech, the hon. gentleman indicated his main reason for opposing the measure at this time is that it would detract from the money available for new home construction. Since the population growth will create a demand for new homes at the rate of 120,000 units a year in perpetuity, will the hon. gentleman indicate when, if ever, we can take money from this desirable purpose and put it to another purpose that is just as desirable?

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF MORTGAGE PROVISIONS TO INCLUDE COMPLETED DWELLINGS

In answer to that question I may say that the time when that can be done will be the time when two things exist. The first will be the time when the federal government can put more money totally into this field, and I do not feel that the government can do that right now. I refer to the time

when the total resources available from the federal treasury for the building of houses are greater.
This is one condition. I think the other is that right now we are vitally concerned with the problem of unemployment. If we succeed in doing what we are trying to do, that is increase the employment level in our manufacturing industries, then at that point we will not be so dependant or so sensitive to the employment provided by the construction industry.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take part in this discussion in order to support the motion introduced by the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Scott).
There are in Canada, at the present time, about 100,000 families which cannot afford homes of minimum standards. Every Canadian, every Canadian family, should have the possibility of buying his own home.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, the program of the Conservative government included legislation which provided loans, at a low rate of interest, to the extent of 90 per cent of the building or purchase cost of low rental housing projects.
There are farm credit provisions which make loans available to farmers for the purchase of farms. We could have housing credit facilities which would help workers who are anxious to buy a house, either in the city or in the suburbs, in a town or even in the country. The inspectors of this housing credit board could recommend the granting of a loan according to the actual value of the buildings at a given location.
For instance, in my riding, many workers would like to buy a house of their own instead of paying rent as they do right now. Is there a finer ambition for any man, even the poorest worker, than to wish to own his home?
If loans were provided on houses which are already built up to a maximum of 90 per cent of the value of the property, those workers would be able to realize their dream, thus killing two birds with one stone. It would be advantageous to house builders and it would create a demand for the services of tradesmen. Considering that the building of a new house requires many hours of labour, there would be fewer unemployed. In addition, new constructions require a lot of materials which are produced by Canadians in Canada and in my riding in particular. That would also improve the labour situation.
National Housing Act
Besides, the construction of new houses entails the purchase of new drapes, new furniture and all kinds of goods. That again would increase employment.
This is why I was saying a moment ago that we would thus kill two birds with one stone.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to dwell at length on this legislation for it is, I think, very important for the Canadian workers, for the workers who live in my county and who would like to own a house; unfortunately, it often happens that whenever they want to buy a house that is already built, their plans are thwarted. This is why I am asking the government to seriously consider this matter and thus make it possible for our workers to have a house of their own, with the help of a loan that could perhaps be similar to loans granted in the agricultural field. Apart from helping them to have a home, it would provide jobs for many unemployed people in Canada.

subtopic: SUGGESTED EXTENSION OF MORTGAGE PROVISIONS TO INCLUDE COMPLETED DWELLINGS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I wish to associate with those who preceded me in order to congratulate you on your appointment to the high office you now hold. It is my first opportunity to take part in the debates of the house.
The motion of the hon. member for Dan-forth (Mr. Scott) is especially related to the re-financing or purchase of housing units already built, so as to enable some people to obtain from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation the necessary funds for that purpose.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the matter is worth thinking over. I cannot say, however, that we can give the matter our unqualified support.
I think that the purpose of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is to promote the building of housing units and to improve their quality.
If this motion were to be adopted without restrictions, the result would probably be that very old houses would change hands; then the number of houses to be built would be reduced while the number of slums, which is already too great in this country, would increase. However, I believe that the proposal put forth by the hon. member for Danforth deserves our consideration.
Taking into account the fact that it is in the first years after a house is built that the

National Housing Act
owner, for various reasons, must sometimes give it up, I am of the opinion that the proposal has some merit.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation could finance the purchase of a house built some years ago, provided it meets the C.M.H.C. standards.
Now, if I make certain restrictions, it is because I cannot accept this proposal straight away.
However, I should like to take this opportunity to outline the situation now existing in Canada. In the province of Quebec, especially in the Saguenay area that I represent, thousands of houses have been built. At the present time, in the Saguenay area, unemployment has reached a rather high level, and municipal and school taxes have increased, so that family heads with low income, who had built a house for their family, must make monthly payments of about $70 including taxes. But, because of present conditions, they are now paying $80, $90 and even more each month for their accommodation. Now, many of them wonder whether they will be able to continue paying this. To my mind, we might bring about some changes so as to allow those people who have made payments for five, six, and even ten years, to re-finance, and even obtain a reduction of their monthly payment.
Mr. Speaker, this will obviously bring about an increase of the interests which will have to be paid by those heads of families, but there again, I know that it has been asked for a long time in the house that the interest rate be reduced. I hope that, in a not too remote future, we might make available to Canadian citizens the necessary means for building a house, a simple dwelling, or a multi-dwelling unit, at an interest rate which would not be prohibitive like the one paid today.
It has been said earlier in this debate that, over a period of twenty or even of twenty five years, people had to pay double the value of the house. That is indeed a fact, and I hope that the house will take that situation into consideration and promote the development of housing in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I know that every minute counts, though I would have had a great deal more to say on the subject. However, I shall resume my seat so that the resolution may be accepted with some reservations.

Mr. Speaker, I would like first of all to tell the

hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Scott) that I myself have bought a house wrapped in a mortgage.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, having heard the remarks made by those who spoke before me, it is readily seen that the principle itself is acceptable, but it is still necessary to consider some statistics.
As was mentioned by a member of the opposition a while ago, it was the intention of the then government, in 1962, to set interest rates which would be acceptable for everybody; it was about time that they should have thought of that because they were the ones who had given the interest rate a little boost, making it jump from 5j- to 6| per cent.
The principle according to which it would be possible to extend the benefits of the act to houses already built was given careful consideration. But has any thought been given to the speculation angle? It has been said that this measure could reduce unemployment, but was the exodus which has taken place in our ridings for many years taken into consideration?
We contributed to lending of close to $2,500,000 on mortgages and the present member for Chambly-Rouville prepared the legal documents for 250 titles.
Since 1958, we have noticed a raise in the interest rates. We are in an urban and semiurban area and, as was mentioned by the hon. member for Toronto-Broadview (Mr. Hahn) a moment ago, many people have moved due to the increase in transportation costs. We have presently in our municipality from 35 to 40 houses whose owners have difficulty meeting the monthly instalments due to the increase in transportation costs.
We considered the matter and we most seriously asked ourselves if financing of houses already built should not be abandoned to the private sector, i.e., banks or insurance companies.
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation made a commendable effort as far as home improvement loans are concerned, and lent money at a reasonable rate in order that the owners may not be compelled to further encumber their properties.
In some areas, new houses were built with a very small down payment through secondary mortgaging.
We could ask ourselves whether we would not be promoting speculation if we refinanced houses already built. As a matter of fact

should we not leave to the private sector the assessment of property values or construction quality.
Please understand that we are not dealing with social aspects, we are only concerned with the construction of houses and the balancing of a precarious budget situation. We would like all Canadians to be enabled to build their own houses. However, Canadians must live according to their means and they will do this only if they buy the property they can afford.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is possible at this time to support the policy advocated by the hon. member for Danforth.
It was stated a while ago that some Canadians could not keep their property. In my opinion, no government whatsoever is responsible for that. When a mortgage is granted at 6 per cent interest, the terms of repayment do not change. However, municipalities have a responsibility so far as taxes are concerned and that is what may alter the terms of repayment.
Having said this about one of the sorest points, that relating to speculation and not the humanitarian aspect, one must come to the conclusion that the whole question should be left to private enterprise, as I said a while ago.
